#4873. The 6 Best Compression Boots to Support Muscle Recovery, Tested by Fitness Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

We turn to these for a enjoyable (and effective) post-workout recovery routine.

MY RECOVERY ROUTINE has included quality time in my compression boots for a few years now. For a lot of guys (myself included) self care is not a strong suit. For many years I went hard until the wheels came off, and eventually I learned I could increase my lower-body blood flow, and thus recover quicker, by using a foam roller. But incorporating compression boots into my post-run regime (even if it is a slightly different recovery stimulus) has forced me to take time for myself and also allowed me to enjoy watching some sports while doing the "right thing" for my body.

While several brands offer compression boots for workout recovery, it's clear to us that Hyperice and Therabody reign supreme. Since our initial 2021 review of Therabody's compression boots, the brand has introduced an innovative and affordable wireless iteration known as the JetBoots Prime. On the Hyperice front, a compact solution called the Normatec Go is an uber-portable compression boot system that targets the calves and allows for easy on-the-go recovery. And most recently it released the Normatec Elites, which have elevated the game with a wireless design.

"Compression boots were initially designed to treat various medical conditions related to poor circulation and fluid retention," explains Dr. Renato Sanchez, PT, DPT, C.S.C.S. Over the last few years, compression therapy has gained popularity in the fitness industry as a muscle recovery tool—especially after the previous popularity of percussion massage guns.

For those who may have doubts regarding how effective compression boots really are in terms of muscle recovery, we understand your concerns. Let's clarify that there is still a significant shortage of scientific research supporting claims about the effectiveness of compression boots in expediting or enhancing the recovery process. (Brands might tell you otherwise, but we only go by the independent studies.) Instead, we can only tell you how we've felt after using them firsthand.

"Compression boots do have value," says MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. "The end result is definitely relaxing—thus allowing my nervous system to down regulate. That down regulation has recovery value."

To simplify the process of choosing from the massive range of options, we've put together a guide to buying compression boots for various individuals. Up next, you'll find our thoroughly tested and vetted backing of the six best compression boots, suitable for every workout routine and budget.

From the moment that the Normatec Elites arrive at your door, fully charged and ready to help you recover within moments, you know that you've made the right choice in compression boot. Normatec has been at the forefront of compression boot technology since it launched in 1998, and has only got better since it was acquired by recovery brand Hyperice in 2020.

I am a fan of how simple it is to get started, just zip your legs into the sleeves and select the compression level and desired treatment time. The attachments begin to inflate in sequence, starting with your feet and moving upwards. For the amount of relief they provide, the sleeves are fairly light, but you can't really move around much one you are zipped up.

There are no external cords necessary, which is nice. The package comes with a charger that can be used to charge both attachments at the same time. It also comes with a travel bag that you can use to pack the attachments if you want to take them on any trips.

Putting these on after an intense run or leg workout has become a ritual, and I struggle to think of any complaints I have with this unit. They are sleek looking, simple to use, and really help elevate your recovery time at home (or on the go).Read More: Normatec Elite Review

We were fans of the Therabody JetBoots when they first released, with a streamlined design eliminating cords and separate controllers. Now the JetBoots Prime from Therabody bring those same benefits we enjoyed for a few hundred dollars less. So we're not going to complain.

These boots are easy to move around the home, so you can throw them on anywhere to enjoy the 20-100 mmHg pressure handsfree. These boots have accompanied us on the couch, in bed, and even inside an airport lounge. It's an untethered experience that's super convenient, whether you're new to compression boots or not. Put 'em on, press the buttons on one leg (they're auto-paired, which we found even more convenient), and the air-massage begins.There is also something nice about being limited to four time intervals (20 minutes, 40 minutes, 60 minutes, continuous) and four pressure levels (25, 50, 75, 100 mmHg). Sometimes minimizing the options makes everything a little more straight forward. This is all managed with the simple control panel on the Primes that's conveniently designed into one of the boots. If you're not wanting to splurge for the Pro system, these are the boots for you.

Perhaps the coolest design of compression boots yet, our editors found the portable Normatec Go boots easy to transport and simple to use. The one downside is that they only cover the calves, so it's not ideal for those looking to tackle hamstring and quad soreness and recovery. But, if you're someone whose calves cry out following a workout and are looking to dip your toes in the world of compression boots without making too significant of an investment, these are an excellent choice.

These boots don't sacrifice on performance even though they're smaller. We found that the Go especially shines following a long run or full day of walking. "I've had to travel for a few races and these sleeves are a great recovery tool that don't take up an entire piece of luggage," says Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM.

Plus, it can be functional to get the compression your calves need without being stuck in a lying position on the couch. The Go's offer a bit more mobility to play video games or work from a laptop–we've even used a pair on an airplane.

For those in search of a full spa experience for their legs, the PRO Plus system from Therabody aims to give it to you, daring to integrate vibration and red light therapy into its compression boots. Like other models on this list, they show up at your door fully charged. Even with all the additional technology, these boots are surprisingly lightweight, and don't feel too bulky on the legs.

The red light therapy isn't a game-changer (although it does make for a cool selling point). But the vibration is a nice addition to the treatment, and while the actual recovery benefits from it may be negligible, it is pleasant. We also like that the Pros can be programmed with your favorite preset settings, so they're locked and loaded whenever you're ready to get a session in.

They also come with two special preset programs you can't get on the Prime or the original JetBoots: Isolation and Interval mode. From there, the customization gets more intense. We're talking adjustable pressure time, hold time, and pressure range that provide the opportunity to work your muscles the best way you see fit at any given moment.

Normatec's Full Body system is practical than most other full-body systems out there. Reason being, this version covers the areas people are more likely to be sore in, like the hips and legs, as well as the arms. Hyperice's attachments here are just better, and the straps make them fairly simple to put on by yourself. The only pain point is if you want to use both arm attachments, you'll likely need someone to help you strap in.

The ability to treat your hips and arms is a big win for anyone looking for a more well-rounded solution. And while compression to this extent doesn't guarantee muscle recovery, a half hour treatment will definitely help you relax after an intense session or even just rough day at the office. (Just note that the arms are pretty restrictive to don; don't expect to type emails comfortably while treating your biceps and triceps.)

The Normatec 3.0 control unit can plug into two attachments at a time, so it is up to you whether you want to treat both legs, two arms, or any other combination of two. For a true full body treatment, you can alternate between sides after your first session is complete.

The Hyperboots were first revealed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and were used by athletes like LeBron James during the games, along with a vest that also featured similar technology. After the reveal, the MH team was excited to get our hands on these, and when we did this summer, we weren’t disappointed.

The Hyperboots, which look more like high-tech, high-top sneakers than boots, show up in a sleek black box emblazoned with the logos for Hyperice and Nike like any other pair of footwear. The boots themselves have a great aesthetic, looking cool enough to even wear on the streets of New York. In order to be used, they are charged with a standard USB-C cable (a welcome sight as opposed to other devices that try to create proprietary chargers).

Let's be clear though, these Hyperboots aren't true compression boots, so you may not get all of the benefits we mentioned above. But you do get a piece of gear that is unique an innovative with sequential air compression combined with targeted heat, which makes it a solid warmup device, as well as a solid late night recovery option, when you want to hit errands as you treat.

Once you’re strapped into the shoes, there are three compression settings, going up to 210 mmHg—more than any other device in this guide. There are also three heat settings going up to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, which is more than you need. “Nike definitely got things right from a tech perspective,” says MH Fitness Director, Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. who got an early pair sent. “The compression and heat is great, especially around the heel. I only wish I was feeling the compression the same on my entire foot.”

The consensus on the Hyperboots is that they are an impressive piece of technology that bring relief to a part of our body that takes a lot of punishment, especially if you are training hard. And while the cost is a little high, these stylish sneakers do help alleviate aches, making them a valid purchase if you have the means. Hyperice’s Normatec Elites have become a regular part of my recovery routine, and I could see the Hyperboots becoming one, too.

The unit of measure that you will see when describing the pressure that these compression boots give is millimeters of mercury (or mmHg). The minimum amount you will commonly see is 20 mmHg, which is a similar amount of pressure that you would get from your standard compression sock, with it going up from there. The ability to adjust compression intensity is essential to accommodate varying recovery needs and your own preferences.

Some products offer more adjustability and levels of compression than others, allowing you to fine-tune your experience to the exact compression you're looking for. Look for boots that offer as much adjustability as possible, with no less than four compression levels.

Consider the convenience of putting on and taking off the compression boots. Look for user-friendly designs with simple controls or automated features that make using and operating the boots—from start to finish—simple and accessible. Wireless capabilities have become a little more prevalent, and obviously offer the simplest and most portable option—though they often come with a heftier price tag

If you plan to use the boots at home or while traveling, consider portability and storage options. Compact designs (such as the Normatec Go) or accompanying carrying cases can make transportation and storage more convenient. And again, the wireless design is key for portability and on-the-go use.

For battery-operated compression boots, evaluate the battery life and charging time. Longer battery life ensures uninterrupted use during recovery sessions, while quick charging capabilities reduce downtime between uses. We recommend looking for a battery life of three hours or more for an optimal experience. While you won't (read: should not) use your boots for three hours in a single session, a long battery life ensures you have to charge them after every session.

Explore any extra features or functionalities offered by the compression boots, such as massage modes, heat therapy, or integration with mobile apps for personalized recovery programs. The Hyperice products on this list feature connectivity with the brand's app, while the Therabody app features Bluetooth connectivity that learns from your use and integrates into Apple Health and Google Fit. Remember, though, that what you're chasing with compression boots should be quality compression. Brands love blending in other traits (red-light therapy, etc.), but don't pay extra for these.

Research the reputation of the brand and read reviews from other users to gauge the effectiveness and reliability of the compression boots. Many brands provide compression boots for post-workout recovery, but our testing has revealed Therabody and Hyperice as the most trusted. Since our initial evaluation in 2021, we have been continuously impressed by the reliability and quality of these two brands.

Being the Fitness and Reviews Editor of Men's Health means I get my hands on every piece of new recovery gear that releases, sometimes before it releases. To build this guide to the best compression boots, I compared the best-selling boots on the market with overlooked classics and newly released options.

Along with Men's Health fitness editors and experts including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, we invested countless hours to put all major compression boot brands to the test by evaluating each model's comfort, fit, ease of use, value, and overall performance. We also sought expertise from physical therapists Renato Sanchez, PT, DPT, C.S.C.S. of Bespoke Treatments San Diego and Dan Giordano, PT, DPT, C.S.C.S. of Bespoke Treatments NYC to understand the role compression can play in recovery and rehabilitation.

Compression boots work by using air pressure to control the blood circulation in your legs.

"As each chamber in the boots fills with air and compresses more tightly, it prevents a large amount of blood from circulating through that part of your body," says Samuel. "So when the boots tighten around your feet first and then your calves, your blood flow to those areas is limited. As this compression continues around your entire leg, you’re left with even more limited blood flow. But just a moment after all that, the chambers methodically deflate, permitting blood to travel first into your thighs, then down through your lower legs, then into your feet."

The theory behind this practice is the onrush of blood will help bring nutrients to help your legs recover efficiently, but this has not been proven for fact.

"There is conflicting evidence that compression devices aid in long term muscle recovery from delayed onset muscle soreness," according to Dr. Sanchez. "However, there has been research that suggests short term relief from exercise induced muscle damage."

Despite the lack of proof, the gentle squeezing of the leg muscles can feel relaxing—even massage-like at times.

To ensure your blood circulation doesn't get cut off Therabody and Hyperice have capped its devices to only reach specific amounts of pressure (measured in mmHG). So as long as you properly place the boots on your legs and use them for the time settings given, your risk of injury is low. Just make sure if you're new to using compression boots you start with the lowest setting first with short periods of time. Then, as you get more comfortable with using your compression boots, you can play with the higher mmHG levels and time settings.

Buying a pair of compression boots is no small investment, which is why we took the time to vet the most trustworthy products above. Painting in broad brushstrokes, compression boots are largely expensive because you're bringing high-level compression therapy tech into to the comfort of your own home.

So with the price points you see with Hyperice and Therabody, you have to consider the amount of research and development needed to help advanced the compression boots while still being easy to use. Features like simple control panels, built-in internal pumps, preset programs, and compression targeting are several examples of tech that's been improved upon in the last few years.

Second to consider is portability, as brands have been able to condense the size to make them relatively easy to move around the house and travel with. Last is safety, as brands have to make sure the compression boots operate within a specific boundary to ensure you receive a tightening effect on your muscles without going too far and potentially causing injury.

Compression boots can be used every day, according to Dr. Giordano. Especially for intense exercisers.

Aim to wait a few hours after any workout, says Samuel, to get the most out of your compression boots. "Removing inflammation too soon after a workout doesn't give your body a chance to adapt to the training stimulus you just created," says Samuel. "Think of compression boots as an ideal way to end a tough training day, instead of using them immediately after a run or workout."

There's another use for them, too. "They are commonly used after intense exercise, but can also be used prior to exercise as part of a warm up routine," says Dr. Sanchez. "I suggest using them for 10-15 minutes pre exercise."

Keep in mind: It’s important to first discuss with a healthcare professional to determine if compression boots are right for you.

#4871. Garmin and Waze just teamed up on a clever new way to keep cyclists safer

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.

The new feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.

As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.

I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.

That’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a big difference.

Of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.

But I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.

The feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin says location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Big Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.

This is cool but requires both a Garmin product and the Waze app. IMHO better to equip new cars and trucks with bicycle and pedestrian detection.

Garmin LiveTrack itself is free for users with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.

There’s obviously one big limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.

But with Waze claiming around 200 million users globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.

Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

#4869. Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

An entire generation of younger women is being educated in the process.

Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause. She didn’t learn anything about it in school, nor from the women in her family. But when she was a teenager, she started noticing her mother’s mood shifting. Around her mid-to-late 40s, “she became much snappier, more easily irritated, and sometimes just seemed angry in a way that felt completely different from the mom I remembered growing up,” she recalls. “I genuinely thought life had simply worn her down.”

Cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle. Once she realized her mother had entered perimenopause, she went down an internet rabbit hole to learn about it. Women were discussing—in detail—what was happening to their bodies on TikTok and Reddit. Some women were going through menopause early, others were seeking answers for their symptoms.

These discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent. In the past, there wasn’t much education—or even real discussion—on what happens to the female body after 40, forcing women to hustle through hot flashes and mood swings behind closed doors.

But within the last few years, there’s been a shift: Gen X women are the first to go through this hormonal transition in the age of social media—and they’re not afraid to talk about their experiences, says Gillan Goddard, MD, an endocrinologist and an adjunct assistant professor of medicine at the NYU Langone Hospital. They’re educating an entire generation of younger women in the process. Posts about brain fog, inconsistent sleep patterns, and unfamiliar-feeling bodies have become the first real health literacy that this generation’s daughters, Gen Zers, have gotten about their own hormonal futures. These small conversations have big implications when it comes to learning more about their future health.

The lack of menopause education starts in classrooms: Almost all U.S. states require teenagers to learn about puberty, reproductive health, and sexual disease prevention through sex education classes. But the content and depth of those classes may not favor women’s health: A 2024 study in the Journal of School Health looked at the state of menstrual health education in U.S. K-12 public schools. Researchers analyzed the education standards from each state’s Department of Education site, searching terms like “menstruation,” “menopause,” “period,” “reproduction,” and “puberty.” It found that menstrual health education—especially menopause—is profoundly rare.

There’s also a lack of menopause education in medical schools. Only 31.3 percent of U.S. ob-gyn residency programs include a menopause curriculum, according to a 2023 study in Menopause. The result resembles a serious disconnect: The transition affects nearly half of the population, but the majority of the doctors tasked with treating menopause have received almost no training on how to do it.

Menopause just isn’t prioritized during residency training. Instead, the “focus during training was placed on surgical skills and labor and delivery responsibilities, both considered more urgent and time-consuming,” says Alyssa Dweck, MD, chief medical officer of Bonafide Health and a Menopause Society Certified Practitioner located in New York City. Ob-gyns can earn certifications in (peri)menopause, from organizations including the Menopause Society and Integrative Women’s Health Institute—but they’re not required. Clinicians should have more comprehensive training in medical school and beyond, says Dr. Dweck. But there should also be more funding and resources for women’s health research for treatment options.

When doctors aren’t familiar with menopause, “mood changes, cognitive changes, and body aches are often misunderstood or ignored,” says Dr. Goddard. This can lead to misdiagnoses, and to women not receiving proper treatment for symptoms caused by menopause. This is pretty common: A 2025 survey conducted by health care company Biote of over 1,000 women ages 30 to 60 in the U.S. found that 39 percent of women have been misdiagnosed and prescribed medication by a provider for conditions like depression.

TikTok and Instagram have filled the menopause education void in the U.S. Conversations about life in menopause have spread awareness about what the condition is actually like, crushing stigmas. This visibility is not only helping younger viewers learn what they can expect later in life—it’s also helping mothers start more health-forward conversations with their daughters.

Milan Parker, 25, has always had open conversations about health with her mom. “She’s always been really honest with me about what she’s going through, even the more personal parts that people sometimes consider taboo,” she says. But social media increased this dynamic tenfold: Parker’s mother underwent a hysterectomy due to fibroids at 48, which made her enter early menopause. Following the surgery, her mother joined a menopause support group on Facebook. “Seeing that there were women all across the country going through similar things made her more open to talking to me about it,” Parker says.

For instance, Parker’s mom finally explained how debilitating her hot flashes really were. (She’d stopped going on trips with her because she was embarrassed about looking sweaty.) “There were times when I thought maybe my mom just didn’t want to go out with me,” she says. “I’m really grateful that she made it something we could actually talk about instead of something that had to stay a secret.”

For daughters, it can be hard to watch their mothers struggle in menopause and not know how to help, but the experience can also help them grow closer. “The emotional experience can be a mix of empathy, grief, anxiety, and closeness,” says Ashley Peña, LCSW, a clinical social worker and the vice president of outpatient operations at Mission Connection.

Even though Cancio’s mom didn’t tell her when she was going through menopause, the experience helped her gain compassion for her mother and better understand her own body. “As a teenager, I honestly thought she was just becoming grumpy or ‘getting old,’ which I feel terrible admitting now,” she says. “As an adult woman, I have so much more empathy.”

Having a raw look at what menopause is actually like—whether through a screen or a conversation with their mother—shapes how younger women view aging and how to prepare themselves for what’s ahead. Hearing that they may one day inevitably experience sleepless nights, sudden anger, brain fog, and the loss of identity can be scary, to say the least. But “open conversation about menopause helps women hear the full scope of menopause experiences and how women dealt effectively with their symptoms,” Dr. Goddard says. It can make the condition sound less scary to younger women.

In fact, growing conversations around menopause can actually inspire younger women to learn about it earlier. “I am seeing patients of all ages, Gen Z included, who have become more inquisitive and engaged in their health overall,” Dr. Dweck says. Some of her young patients have told her they’ve already started talking to their older relatives about menopause and hormone health. They’re also more open about discussing fertility and egg freezing.

Even though menopause is now common dinner table conversation, the root of the (non-communication) issue still needs to be fixed. “The only way we normalize talking about women’s health is by talking about it,” Cancio says. “Ask questions, stay curious, and don’t be afraid to learn from women who have already been through it.”

Mothers going through (peri)menopause can have a series of casual conversations about it with their kids. (The earlier, the better.) They can keep the conversation casual and tailored to the child’s developmental age. For instance, moms with children under the age of 13 can briefly mention that they’re “going through a body change.” Then, as the kids get older, they can talk more openly about what they’re experiencing, says Dr. Dweck. Encouraging their children to ask questions about menopause can also build empathy and normalize conversations surrounding health.

On the flip side, Parker wants Gen Z women to pay attention to what their mothers are going through, and not wait until the right moment to spark a conversation. “Having those conversations with my mom has made that feel a lot less scary and a lot more human,” she says. “Every stage of life comes sooner than you think, so it’s worth paying attention to your health long before you feel like you have to.”

Cancio didn’t feel like she could have those conversations with her mom, which is part of what inspired her to start making content around women’s health topics for younger women. “I started thinking about the girl who was sitting at home Googling something because she was too embarrassed to ask her mom, or the girl who thought something was wrong with her because nobody had ever explained that what she was experiencing was normal,” she says.

Even though the way that Gen Z is learning about menopause isn’t perfect—whether through a viral post or their mother—it’s still a step in the right direction. By doing her part, Cancio hopes to have a completely different relationship with her future daughter “where no topic about her body is off limits and she never feels like she has to search for answers alone.”

#4868. Beef Prices Are at Record Highs—But There’s a Smart Way You Can Save Cash and Score Quality Meat

Editor’s Note: When I originally reported this article in 2014, a pound of ground beef cost roughly $3.50. Now that same amount of protein costs you $6.75. But nothing about buying beef wholesale has changed: You will still save more money over time if you purchase an eighth, a quarter, a half, or even a whole cow given you have the upfront cash and deep freezer space to store it all. (A quarter of a cow from the same farm I purchased mine now costs $1,100, in case you were wondering.)

And, if you can spring for grass-fed beef, there’s been more recent published research to show that it might be healthier for you than the grain-fed variety. In 2022, South Korean researchers found that grass-fed beef contained a healthier fatty acid profile than grain-fed beef. Same goes for a 2026 study published in the Journal of Animal Science.

While eating healthier is great, doing so has to taste amazing too. Luckily that hasn’t changed about grass-fed beef either.

THE COW I ate was born in rural Pennsylvania. Cathy Pomanti, the owner of Sugar Hill Farm, midwifed my calf into the world. Pomanti raises grass-fed organic Scottish Highland Cows, a shaggy breed yielding meat that’s among the tastiest on the planet. On one farm visit, my fiancee saw a highlander, went quiet, and then said, “I don’t want to eat them. I want to hug them.” But I was hungry for a cow to call my own.

As a pleasure-seeking meat eater, disappointed by grain-fed supermarket beef. Rib eyes require a slick of steak sauce to taste meaty. Ground beef has a tacky, greasy consistency. Tenderloin, even with tender care, always leaves me underwhelmed. So I decided to stop complaining about mass-market beef and find a rancher. I wanted to know my cattle producer. I wanted to know my cow.

My cow never had a name; Pomanti can’t bring herself to name cows headed for slaughter. But he did have a good life. My cow spent his first 10 months growing strong on his mother’s milk, sticking close by her side. Then Pomanti separated my cow and his mother into different pens. My cow bawled. His mother mooed. It was for the best. Once Mom stopped producing milk, the two were reunited, but my cow now preferred delicious, nutritious grass.

Over the next year and a half, my cow grew an impressive coat of thick, coarse hair. Because he wouldn’t be subjected to the diseases and indignities of the industrial feedlot, he didn’t need antibiotics or growth hormones. Those substances wouldn’t end up in me or my fiancée, either.

Last October, my cow was loaded onto a truck and taken to Rising Spring Meat Company, an organic butcher outside State College, Pennsylvania. There he was held in a pen, calm and comfortable, until he was humanely shot in the head. The carcass was then halved and hung in a cooler to dry-age, a process that helps tenderize the meat, for about 14 days. Next my cow was cut into pieces, vacuum-sealed, and delivered to Pomanti.

She summoned me for the handoff. Out of her massive freezer units she pulled bags bursting with marrow bones, globular ground beef portions, and a tenderloin the size of Popeye’s forearm. I drove the box of beef back home that day, dreaming of meals to come, under a sky with clouds that looked like heifers.

AS A TYPICAL American, you ate a hefty 51 pounds of beef last year, the USDA says. That’s roughly the equivalent of 65 T-bones or 204 quarter-pound burger patties.

The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association notes that less than 1 percent of beef sold at retail is labeled as grass-fed. During the “finishing,” the animal begins to lay down more fat in relation to muscle and bone growth, says Cindy Daley, Ph.D., who studies beef at California State University.

Until the 1950s, ranchers finished cattle exclusively on grass. But industrial producers realized that grain feeding improved fat marbling while cutting the days until slaughter. After decades of eating the stuff, we now prefer fattier beef. But at the same time, our rates of diseases linked to inflammation rose.

Could grain-fed cows and inflammation be connected? A 2011 Irish study found that people who replaced their regular red meat with three weekly servings of grass-fed red meat for a month improved their inflammation-fighting omega-3 fatty acid profiles by 37 percent over those of people who ate the same amount of grain-finished red meat.

Though the diet studies are too small to be conclusive, a 2010 research review led by Daley found that grass-fed beef outclassed grain-fed nutritionally, with triple the immune-boosting vitamin E, up to five times the heart-healthy omega-3 fatty acids, and seven times the antioxidant carotenoids.

If grass-fed beef was going to treat me better, I needed to return the favor. So I began contacting chefs. The recipes that follow taught me key kitchen skills, but they also taught me something deeper: If you know your beef, you love it even more.

THERE’S A CERTAIN comfort in dissociating yourself from the animal you’re eating for dinner. If you don’t think about where on the cow’s body the meat comes from, you don’t have to contemplate the death and dismemberment involved in its trip to your plate. The oxtail, however, made a very specific statement about its origins. It came to me in three pieces, which, because of my morbid curios- ity, I arranged to reconstruct the entire appendage. I imagined my cow using it to swat flies. It wasn’t simply a meal. It was a sacrifice.

Alice Waters, executive chef of Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, and founder of the Edible Schoolyard Project, recommends cooking oxtail in a classic braise. “With grain-fed beef, you’re tasting a richness and tenderness, but it’s not the real flavor,” Waters says. “It’s like cooking vegetables with a lot of butter: You can’t taste the vegetables.” Her technique, inspired by a recipe from Zuni Café in San Francisco, matches the beautiful beefiness of the rustic cut while also turning it fork-tender.

Bonus: You can apply the same braising technique to other tough bone-in cuts your purveyor may pass along, such as shanks or short ribs.

2 lb grass-fed oxtails1 Tbsp Kosher salt4 cups beef stock2 Tbsp olive oil1 ¾ cups red wine2 bay leaves1 small head garlic, halved crosswise1 sprig thyme3 black peppercorns1 large carrot, peeled and roughly chopped3 celery stalks, roughly chopped1 medium yellow onion, quartered1 cup drained canned tomatoes, roughly chopped

1. For the best flavor, salt the oxtails two days before cooking.

2. Trim the oxtails of excess fat. In a medium saucepan, cook the stock over medium heat until reduced by half, about 30 minutes.

3. In a skillet, heat the oil on medium. Pat the oxtails dry and brown them, 3 to 4 minutes. Set aside. Wipe the skillet, add the wine, stir, and cook it down by half, about 5 minutes. Add the stock.

4. Preheat the oven to 300°F. In a roasting pan, add the remaining ingredients; add stock to cover by a third. Simmer on medium low. Cover.

5. Place the pan in the oven and cook 3 to 4 hours. Then crack the lid and cook until the meat is very tender, another 20 to 30 minutes. Serve oxtails with sauce. Makes 8 servings

I NEEDED TO do something special with the most prestigious cut of my cow: the 14-pound standing rib roast. The meal should be special but also very simple, says Donald Link, owner and executive chef of Cochon and Butcher in New Orleans. Anything too fussy would only detract from its intense, glorious beefiness.

For maximum flavor, you want to cook this behemoth roast only to medium rare, Link told me. Because the cut is so large, the preparation and resting stages are critical. If the meat is too cold before it enters the oven, it’ll be raw in the center when it exits. If you carve into it immediately after cooking, you’ll lose a reservoir of delicious juices. Patience is paramount.

And the rewards are well worth the wait: “Good grass-fed beef tastes cleaner. You don’t have that heavy feeling in your gut after you eat it,” Link says. I heard similar accolades from the friends and family members I invited over to dinner. In fact, most people said the steaks, liver, or carne asada I’d served them tasted “like beefier beef” and “less greasy.” One guest who tasted the rib roast said she woke up the morning after our dinner fantasizing about the beef from the night before.

1 grass-fed beef rib roast (14 lb)Olive oil

1. To promote even doneness, remove the roast from the refrigerator 2 hours before cooking.

2. Place the roast on a wire rack set on a baking sheet. The last 30 minutes prior to cooking, place a fan in front of the meat to dry excess moisture and foster caramelization.

3. Preheat the oven to 450°F. Lightly rub the roast on all sides with olive oil and then liberally coat it with salt and freshly ground pepper. Set it back on the wire rack atop the baking sheet and place it in the oven.

4. Cook until well browned on the outside, about 20 minutes. Lower the heat to 275°F and continue to cook until a digital thermometer inserted into the center of the roast reads 140°F, about 2 hours. Remove the roast and let it rest until it’s almost at room temperature, about 45 minutes.

5. Serve with roasted potatoes and a simple salad. Makes 20 to 25 servings

OF THE 51 pounds of cow you ate last year, about half was ground. Here’s a scary fact: U.S. ground beef is not easily traced and may not even be from the United States, a 2013 review in Meat Science reveals. All the more reason to buddy up to a rancher.

You can make a grass-fed beef burger (I did), but you’d be depriving your tastebuds if you didn’t venture beyond familiar ground. “Grass-fed beef is very lean by nature. Grinding beef for burgers involves adding fat, and if you’re using grass-fed, you lose something,” says Sang Yoon, executive chef of Father’s Office and Lukshon in L.A. That something, he says, is the herbaceous flavor imparted by the cow’s diet. Make larb instead, Yoon says. This Southeast Asian dish packs a barrage of fresh herbs to flatter grass-fed beef.

1 Tbsp uncooked jasmine rice6 Tbsp peanut oil12 oz grass-fed ground beef1 shallot, minced2 garlic cloves, sliced2 fresh Thai chiles, thinly sliced1 Tbsp palm sugar2 Tbsp fish sauce¼ cup lime juice1 head cabbage, leaves separated½ cilantro leaves½ mint leaves½ Thai basil leaves4 scallions, sliced

1. In a small pan on medium heat, toast the rice, stirring often. Cool and grind the rice to a fine powder in a clean coffee or spice grinder.

2. In a wok or big cast-iron skillet, heat the oil on medium high until it shimmers. Add the beef; cook, stirring occasionally, until it begins to brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Add the shallot, garlic, chiles, palm sugar, and fish sauce.

3. Remove from the heat and add the lime juice and rice powder. Stir well and season with salt.

4. Let the mixture cool slightly before serving. Spoon the mixture into individual cabbage cups and garnish with herbs and scallions. Makes 6 to 8 servings

MARC FORGIONE, OWNER and executive chef of Restaurant Marc Forgione in New York City, told me I should start by not cooking the beef at all. “The best way to experience grass-fed beef, because it’s so lean, is to eat it raw,” says Forgione.

When I asked him if it was dangerous to eat DIY steak tartare, Forgione told me that as long as the beef is high in quality and its temperature never rises above 40°F for longer than 40 minutes, your risk of illness will be very low, he says. And Pomanti, for her part, says bacterial contamination among her cattle is vir- tually nonexistent. (It pays to know your source.)

So I sharpened my knives for a rare opportunity. The result was a luscious tartare that topped variations I’ve tasted at the country’s top steakhouses.

1 Tbsp minced onion1 Tbsp minced cornichons1 tsp minced parsley2 anchovies, minced½ Tbsp Dijon mustard2 or 3 dashes Tabasco sauce2 tsp Worcestershire sauce½ cup, plus 2 Tbsp olive oil1 lb grass-fed beef tenderloinWarm toast

1. In a small bowl, mix the onion, parsley, cornichons, and anchovies. Reserve.

2. In a blender or food processor, add the mustard, Tabasco, Worcestershire, and 2 Tbsp olive oil. Puree, gradually adding the remaining olive oil until emulsified. Reserve.

3. Place the tenderloin in the freezer for about 5 minutes for easier cutting. Then, working quickly, slice it into ¼-inch-thick pieces.

4. In a medium serving bowl, combine the meat with the reserved ingredients. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Mix well.

5. Chill in the fridge for 10 minutes before serving atop warm toast. Makes 8 servings as an appetizer

WHEN MY TOUR of the special cuts was complete, I dug for the last of the T-bones that were stashed aside the cow’s heart (yes, the heart) in the freezer. Steaks were the first cuts I cooked, and I still craved them. Naomi Pomeroy, the executive chef of Beast in Portland, Oregon, had taught me to sear them to a juicy medium rare. She’s a pro; she cooks grass-fed beef exclusively.

I preheated my oven to 350°F and placed a cast-iron skillet over medium heat. I cranked some freshly ground black pepper and scattered kosher salt over each side of the steak. Then I added a good knob of butter to the skillet, allowed it to melt, and followed it with the steak and a few sprigs of parsley and thyme. I listened for the sizzling to subside, awaiting the aroma of a baseball field on a hot summer day. Those signs told me it was time to flip the meat and then slide it into the oven, skillet and all. There it basked for five minutes until the interior temperature reached 122°F. Out of the oven it came. I then basted it reverently with the rest of the melted butter, tented some aluminum foil over the skillet, and let it rest for what seemed like an eternity. Okay, five minutes. And then I savored every last juicy, earthy, hearty, powerful, tender bite. The celebration of my cow was complete.

Yes, grass-fed beef costs more money than the grain-finished variety, but you’re making that investment to enjoy superior meat that is less fatty, more nutrient-dense, better for your body, and certainly better on the palate.

And if you purchase your grass-fed beef in bulk, so much the better. It can be less expensive than grass-fed cuts you’d find in the store, for one thing. There’s also something deeply comfort- ing about possessing a large amount of premium meat. (Zombie apocalypse be damned!) But because you know the life of your cow, and the rancher who raised that animal, you also want to honor that cow in death. It’s not just dinner. It’s your duty.

#4867. The new BMW i3 just proved how efficient an EV can be after a nearly 3,700-mile road trip

Who says long EV road trips mean hours at charging stations? BMW drove the new i3 for over 3 days, covering nearly 3,700 miles, and it took less than 3 hours of charging.

BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.

The Paneurpeana, as it’s called, is considered the benchmark for range and charging speed. The route begins at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe you can reach by car, and ends in Tarifa, Spain, the southernmost point of mainland Europe.

BMW drove the new i3 50 xDrive for a total of 3,658 miles (5,886.7 km) across eight countries and spent just 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds charging at an average of 275 kW.

The performance beat the previous record by more than seven hours, according to Mike Reichelt, head of BMW’s Neue Klasse

BMW said the charging points were not predetermined and that it had to account for external factors such as weather and traffic jams.

The new i3 was impressively efficient during the trip, consuming an average of just 12.5 kWh per 100 km, beating its official WLTP combined energy consumption of 18-13.4 kWh/100 km.

BMW said the trip took 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes, with an average speed of 79.7 km/h, and that the i3 was charged exclusively at public charging points across national charging networks.

The vehicle was driven at all times by a single driver and was not modified in any way, in terms of hardware or software, from the standard i3 available for purchase.

BMW’s new i3 uses a 108.7 kWh battery and Gen6 eDrive system that provides a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

With a drag coefficient of just 0.21, the new i3 is the most aerodynamically efficient BMW vehicle to date.

In the US, BMW said the new 2027 i3 50 xDrive will offer an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 468 miles.

With an 800V architecture, the electric sedan can add nearly 262 miles (423 km) of range (WLTP) in about 10 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds up to 400 kW. In the US, the i3 has a built-in NACS port.

#4866. 45 AD-Approved International Interior Photographers to Know for Your Next Project Abroad

They jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Read on to discover top talents working in Europe, Asia, Oceania, North Africa, South America, and Canada.

Born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and currently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography. His images often center around the collected objects that make a space personal and give it life.

A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.

With Harry Nuriev, Festen, and Bernard Dubois among his collaborators, Ludovic Balay is no stranger to interiors with a point of view. The Paris photographer’s roster also includes Halleroed, adding another distinctive design voice to the picture.

The drawing room of a Notting Hill home designed by Olivia Williams.

Henry Bourne’s photographs open a window into creative people’s private worlds. The UK photographer’s interiors and portrait work includes subjects such as John Pawson, Faye Toogood, Luca Guadagnino, and Rose Uniacke.

A London townhouse designed by AD100 designer Leonora Hamill

Helen Cathcart brings a painterly, atmospheric quality to her work, which has resonated with some of the world’s hottest brands, designers, and publications. Cathcart’s photos of interiors, in particular, proffer serenity and calm through their tonality.

The Row, Lemaire, and a host of AD interiors: François Coquerel’s portfolio is in very good company. The Paris photographer moves between fashion and design, with Massimo Adario and Oitoemponto among his architectural collaborators.

Designer Luca Cipelletti delivers architectural precision and material opulence to an art collector’s Porta Nuova apartment.

Partners in life and work, Michael Depasquale and Martina Maffini count industry names like Dimore Studio, Nilufar Gallery, and JW Anderson among their clients. The duo splits their time between Paris and Milan and injects dynamism into each shoot that becomes evident in the final, glossy-ready results.

A villa in New Zealand by Patterson Associates.

Simon Devitt doesn’t stop at photographing architecture: fine art photo books, exhibitions, and workshops also fill his calendar. Based in Wellington, he has worked with Fearon Hay, Shigeru Ban, and Olson Kundig, documenting buildings across New Zealand and beyond.

Joseph Dirand designs rooms; his brother Adrien photographs them, including the architect’s Paris apartment for AD. Also based in Paris, Adrien contributed photography to the book Joseph Dirand Interior. A creative family, to say the least.

Inside the Paris headquarters of ACNE studios

Having started his career in fashion, Dol Maillot is as beloved for his street style shots and travel photography as he is for his interiors. Born in the South of France, the globetrotting artist now lives in Paris.

A Kelly Behun apartment at London’s Whiteley hotel is just one reason to linger over Veerle Evens’s portfolio. The London photographer moves between interiors, food, and travel, with HBA Residential, Owl Design, and Christian Bense among her collaborators.

A color-drenched home in the Canary Islands.

Some interiors tell you as much about their owners as a portrait might. Miguel Flores-Vianna seeks out those personal worlds, bringing his curiosity not just to interiors but also to his books, including Haute Bohemians and Haute Bohemians Greece. Armchair travelers, settle in.

Join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Learn more

Inside the Paris apartment of Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, as seen in AD France.

Among international interior photographers, Jérôme Galland ups the ante with his photos through a combination of striking contrasts, dramatic angles, and an appreciation of scale. French châteaus, Italian palazzos, and Greek villas all appear at their most grand through his lens.

Venetian interiors and Moroccan retreats make tempting subjects: Kasia Gatkowska’s portfolio travels well. The Amsterdam-based photographer has worked with Vincenzo De Cotiis, Vincent Van Duysen, Axel Vervoordt, and Massimo Adario, among others.

The home of the ABC Concept founders in Karuizawa, Japan.

Kenzo Takada’s Paris home is just one stop in Mitchell Geng’s portfolio. The Tokyo photographer also captured a colorful Hong Kong residence for Vogue Hong Kong and includes architecture, interiors, and hospitality in his photographic itinerary.

Film buffs may recognize Luca Guadagnino, the Italian director, producer, and screenwriter behind films such as Call Me By Your Name; design lovers will know his interiors too. Milan photographer Giulio Ghirardi has worked with the multihyphenate, shooting his interior design projects, and has also turned his lens to the work of Pierre Yovanovitch, Kelly Wearstler, Rodolphe Parente, and Augusta Hoffman.

A kitchen by AKB Design in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec

Whether she is shooting portraits, food, travel, or interiors, Sylvie Li’s commercial and editorial images build a narrative. Just look at how she commemorates the marriage of old and new in this renovated Montreal apartment which appeared in AD.

The reception room of the barn on designer Jean-Louis Denoit’s watercress farm in France.

If Laura Gonzalez, Hugo Toro, and Pierre Yovanovitch feature on your list of design heroes, Stephan Julliard’s portfolio warrants a visit. The Paris photographer has worked with all three, as well as Jean-Louis Deniot, Kelly Wearstler, and Greg Natale.

Designer Meg Sharpe turns a traditional warren of rooms into an airy idyll where livability and flair are winsome bedfellows

Having shot for Dimorestudio, MacGuffin, Icon, and—hello, AD—Kyle Knodell has a knack for producing interior photos filled with life. At AD, we’ve tapped him to photograph Samantha Angelo and Peter Ostrega in their LES home.

The Paris apartment belonging to Gregoire Marot and Thomas Dupré de St Maur, designed with help of their friend the designer Eric Allart

Spain and Uruguay make appealing bookends for Ricardo Labougle’s practice. In between, his lens takes in interiors, gardens, and portraits, with the work of Jacques Grange, Vincent Van Duysen, Studio KO, and Michael S. Smith among its subjects.

A Stockholm apartment designed by Studio Escapist

From OMA’s architecture to Max Lamb’s furniture, Erik Lefvander moves easily between subjects, thrilling design enthusiasts. The Stockholm photographer’s collaborators also include Halleroed, Sabine Marcelis, and Sophie Dries.

Tour a London pied-à-terre by Studio Ashby that’s a dazzling foray into maximalism.

“Uplifting” is the best way to describe Kensington Leverne’s photography, thanks to the softness and warmth that her images exude. Whether the interiors she shoots are palatial or cozy, Leverne is able to evoke a sense of intimacy within each space.

A bedroom in Stockholm’s Ett Hem boutique hotel.

Magnus Mårding takes a natural approach, whether the subject is a person, a car, or an interior. Based in Stockholm, he has worked with Ilse Crawford, Michael S. Smith, and Olson Kundig. Different subjects, one curious eye.

Giulia Maretti can help set the scene as well as photograph it. The Bologna- and Berlin-based MAGI Studio cofounder combines photography, styling, and art direction, and has worked with the likes of MIDE Architetti and Studio Bosko.

A New York townhouse designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, Grace Fuller Marroquin, and Leonora Hamill

Gabriel Chipperfield and Laura de Gunzburg transformed their 19th-century London flat, blending contemporary softness with crisp minimalism.

Multiple shoots for AD and Vogue that show the English country manors and London town houses of the UK’s top celebrities and creatives fill Kate Martin’s portfolio. She adapts her eye for fashion editorial to interiors and portraits with ease.

Nicolas Matheus’s photos have graced the covers of countless international design magazines, depicting chic French apartments, sunny Spanish casas, coastal Cape Town villas, and more. His work in and around the Mediterranean is particularly gorgeous.

Still-life arrangements of smaller objects within larger spaces populate Alice Mesguich’s Instagram feed, showcasing her penchant for capturing styled vignettes as well as corners and niches she finds interesting.

Fans of Ashley Montgomery, Sam Sacks, and Ali Budd may already have Lauren Miller’s images on their inspiration boards. The Toronto photographer captures interiors and still lifes, with work appearing in AD and House & Garden.

Balmore House in North London, designed by Studio 163

Architecture buffs will find familiar names in Peter Molloy’s orbit: O’Donnell + Tuomey, Grafton Architects, and Carmody Groarke, for starters. The London photographer has also worked with McLaren.Excell, keeping the built environment firmly in the frame.

In AD100 designer Vincenzo De Cotiis’s 15th-century Italian palazzo, a breccia baixa marble was chosen for its resemblance to the palazzo’s original ceiling, shown in this bath along with a circa 1895 Carlo Bugatti chair.

Textured surfaces—plasterwork, fabric, timber, you name it—are the first thing noticed in any interior shot by Martin Morrell, making him a favorite of designers like Vincenzo de Cotiis and Studio Peregalli. His full list of both editorial and advertising clients reads as a who’s who of brand and media.

A dining area in the famed Casa de Canoas, a Brazilian modernist landmark designed by Oscar Niemeyer. Parente shot a campaign for Zara Home here.

Fran Parente travels his São Paulo–New York circuit with some excellent design company. Studio Arthur Casas, Studio MK27, Studio Mellone, and Isay Weinfeld figure among his collaborators, while hospitality, travel, and food broaden his view beyond architecture.

The pool area at the Desert Rock Resort in Saudi Arabia.

BIG. Kengo Kuma. Heatherwick Studio. Ema Peter’s collaborator list could double as an architecture lover’s hot list. Working between Vancouver and Los Angeles, she doesn’t just specialize in architecture; she also photographs residential interiors, including projects involving Studio Paolo Ferrari.

Proctor photographed the Brown Drawing Room at Blickling Hall in Norfolk as the house was being ‘put to sleep,’ a custom that involves draping the furniture when the visitor season ends, to allow the collections in the house to have some respite from the elements.

His intimate images of artists’ spaces and decorative arts workshops suggest Oskar Proctor enjoys looking behind the scenes. Working across London, New York, and Los Angeles, he has shot the work of Soane Britain, Vanderhurd, and Jermaine Gallacher, among other design-world names.

A penthouse at One Park Drive, the Herzon & de Meuron building at London’s Canary Wharf.

From the Aman New York to the Janu Tokyo, Robert Rieger’s portfolio makes a compelling case for checking in. The Berlin photographer also counts David Thulstrup, Vincent Van Duysen, and Herzog & de Meuron among his collaborators.

Designer Jacques Garcia’s 17th-century apartment in Paris.

Matthieu Salvaing’s book, Interior Voyages, lives up to its name, taking readers through homes as individual as their inhabitants. The Paris photographer’s travels encompass tropical retreats and historic residences, inviting readers to consider how different home can look around the world.

The bedroom of a New York townhouse designed by Greg Natale.

If your design tastes travel from Flack Studio to Kelly Wearstler, Anson Smart’s portfolio connects the dots. The Sydney photographer also captures interiors by Arent & Pyke and Greg Natale, alongside hospitality and lifestyle assignments.

An apartment in Naples, Italy, designed by FADD Architects.

Architecture training gave Valentina Sommariva an insider’s introduction to the spaces she photographs. Objects get their moment, too, in the work of this Milan talent who also creates fine art projects that combine photography and video. Patricia Urquiola, Studiopepe, and Elisa Ossino Studio are among her collaborators.

The guest bedroom in Tarek Shamma’s London apartment.

Interiors by Child Studio and Holloway-Li make for quite the photographic playground. Working between London and New York, Felix Speller has photographed both, with Studio Hagen Hall and Lina Ghotmeh also among his other design subjects.

A London apartment designed by Douglas Mackie.

If your design references lean British, put Astrid Templier on your radar. The London photographer’s collaborators include Guy Goodfellow, Douglas Mackie, Elicyon, and Rosanna Bossom—a roster that should resonate with fans of the English interior.

A private holiday home in Tuscany, Italy, designed by Vincenzo De Cotiis.

The kitchen in Nate Berkus and Jeremiah Brent’s home in Portugal.

Trevor Tondro’s command of color and mood brings a lively quality to his interiors photography. With early experience assisting both Philip-Lorca diCorcia and Martyn Thompson, he maximizes both artificial and natural light, always finding more than one way into a room.

Historic Castle Howard in North Yorkshire, London

If you find Simon Upton’s list of subjects resembles your decorating bookshelf, that’s understandable. Rose Uniacke, Rita Konig, Michael S. Smith, and Stephen Sills are among the talents whose work the UK-based photographer has captured across continents.

Devotees of Belgian design, take note. Antwerp-based Frederik Vercruysse has worked with Axel Vervoordt, Vincent Van Duysen, and Muller Van Severen—a particularly appealing trio for anyone whose saved images run from contemplative interiors to playful furniture.

This home in the Swiss Alps by activist Nachson Mimran and AD100 talent Francis Kéré graced the cover of AD’s January 2025 issue.

A farmhouse-inspired Manhattan apartment or a chalet in Megève? Cassie Floto Warner has photographed both for AD, including Amanda Seyfried’s New York apartment and a retreat by Elliott Barnes. The Paris-based photographer’s portfolio makes staying in sound particularly appealing.

The living room of a Venetian palazzo by architect Luca Bombassei

Although he works all over the globe, Watson now lives in Dublin, where he was born.

#4864. Tennis is Aces for Healthy Aging

There’s good reason why the United States Tennis Association calls it “the world’s healthiest sport.”

If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research shows that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

“Tennis is a whole-body sport,” says sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”

You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin says.

And those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

When you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin says. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin says. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is important as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

Studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin says. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.
